subject: adult-health-surgery
title: Hip, femur and knee injuries: high-yield principles for NEET-PG and INI-CET

steps.tx: Hip and femur injuries in older adults are time-critical. A **displaced intracapsular femoral neck fracture** disrupts the blood supply to the femoral head, so **avascular necrosis** is a major risk. Surgery, usually fixation or arthroplasty, is needed promptly once the patient is medically fit. Pain on internal rotation and inability to straight-leg raise after a fall suggest hip pathology even when plain films look normal.

steps.tx: When plain radiographs are normal but a hip fracture is suspected, **MRI** is the best next investigation. Early intracapsular fractures can be radiographically occult. MRI shows bone marrow oedema and fracture lines that X-rays miss, and it is highly sensitive. Repeating plain films in two weeks is not the right first step, because it delays diagnosis and surgery.

rows: Normal X-ray, groin pain, cannot bear weight

steps.tx: A long lie on the floor, often more than several hours, can cause **rhabdomyolysis**. Muscle breakdown releases **myoglobin**, potassium and phosphate. Very high creatine kinase, dark urine and rising creatinine point to rhabdomyolysis with acute kidney injury. Early, adequate intravenous fluids and monitoring of urine output protect the kidneys. Hyperkalaemia needs urgent ECG monitoring and treatment.

steps.tx: A knee injury with **gross instability** may be a **knee dislocation**. A cool, pale foot, absent distal pulses and reduced ankle-brachial index mean **arterial compromise**, most often from popliteal artery injury. This is a limb-threatening emergency. Urgent vascular surgical referral and angiography are needed, because ischaemia can cause irreversible damage within hours. Intact sensation does not exclude vascular injury.

steps.tx: Acute knee pain with a pivoting injury, a pop and rapid effusion suggests an **anterior cruciate ligament** tear. A positive Lachman test supports this, and normal X-rays exclude fracture as the main cause. **MRI** of the knee is the best next investigation. It shows ligaments, menisci and cartilage without radiation. Patellar dislocation in adolescents may leave a visible osteochondral flake on X-ray and needs separate assessment.

steps.tx: In a child or adolescent with a limp, hip or knee pain and an obese body habitus, **slipped capital femoral epiphysis** must be excluded. Reduced internal rotation and external rotation of the leg on hip flexion are classic signs. Management is **non-weight-bearing** with urgent orthopaedic referral, because displacement can compromise the femoral head blood supply and cause avascular necrosis. Manipulation or steroid injection is not appropriate.

steps.tx: Before surgery for a hip fracture, check haemoglobin, renal function and clotting. Anaemia reduces the reserve to tolerate operative blood loss, so **crossmatched blood** should be prepared without delaying surgery. Normal creatinine and INR mean no major coagulopathy barrier. Surgery should not be postponed simply until haemoglobin normalises. Raised creatinine or potassium needs correction and monitoring first.
